references.authors: Sullivan JL
references.title: Iron and the sex difference in heart disease risk
references.finding: Proposed the 'iron hypothesis': higher stored iron in men and postmenopausal women explains their higher heart disease risk, and suggested phlebotomy as a test.

references.authors: Zacharski LR, Chow BK, Howes PS, et al.
references.title: Reduction of iron stores and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with peripheral arterial disease: a randomized controlled trial
references.finding: FeAST: phlebotomy to lower ferritin did not significantly reduce all-cause death (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.67-1.08) or death plus MI and stroke (HR 0.88, 0.72-1.07).

references.authors: Zacharski LR, Chow BK, Howes PS, et al.
references.title: Decreased cancer risk after iron reduction in patients with peripheral arterial disease: results from a randomized trial
references.finding: FeAST secondary analysis: iron reduction (mean ferritin ~80 vs ~123 ng/mL) was associated with fewer new visceral cancers (HR 0.65, 0.43-0.97).

references.authors: Depalma RG, Hayes VW, Chow BK, et al.
references.title: Ferritin levels, inflammatory biomarkers, and mortality in peripheral arterial disease: a substudy of the Iron (Fe) and Atherosclerosis Study (FeAST) Trial
references.finding: In a FeAST substudy, ferritin correlated with IL-6 and hsCRP, and higher ferritin tracked with mortality, illustrating ferritin's overlap with inflammation.

references.authors: Hu FB
references.title: The iron-heart hypothesis: search for the ironclad evidence
references.finding: JAMA editorial accompanying FeAST arguing that conclusive ('ironclad') evidence for the iron-heart hypothesis was still lacking.

references.authors: Edgren G, Nyrén O, Melbye M
references.title: Cancer as a ferrotoxic disease: are we getting hard stainless evidence?
references.finding: JNCI editorial accompanying the FeAST cancer analysis, questioning how firm the evidence is that iron reduction prevents cancer.

references.authors: Gill D, Del Greco M F, Walker AP, et al.
references.title: The Effect of Iron Status on Risk of Coronary Artery Disease: A Mendelian Randomization Study-Brief Report
references.n: ~60,800 CAD cases and 123,500 controls (two-sample Mendelian randomization)
references.finding: Genetically higher iron status was associated with slightly LOWER coronary artery disease risk (OR 0.94 per SD serum iron).

references.authors: Liu Y, Clarke R, Bennett DA, et al.
references.title: Iron Status and Risk of Heart Disease, Stroke, and Diabetes: A Mendelian Randomization Study in European Adults
references.n: UK Biobank plus consortia with 181,522 CAD and 80,154 T2D cases (Mendelian randomization)
references.finding: Genetically higher iron biomarkers were modestly protective for coronary disease (7-14% lower risk per SD) but raised type 2 diabetes risk.

references.authors: Wang X, Fang X, Zheng W, et al.
references.title: Genetic Support of A Causal Relationship Between Iron Status and Type 2 Diabetes: A Mendelian Randomization Study
references.finding: Genetically higher serum iron (OR 1.07), ferritin (OR 1.19) and transferrin saturation (OR 1.06) were associated with higher type 2 diabetes risk.

references.authors: Daghlas I, Gill D
references.title: Genetically predicted iron status and life expectancy
references.n: Mendelian randomization using parental lifespan GWAS
references.finding: Each SD of genetically higher serum iron corresponded to 0.7 fewer years of parental lifespan and lower odds of reaching the 90th age percentile (OR 0.81).

references.authors: Gill D, Benyamin B, Moore LSP, et al.
references.title: Associations of genetically determined iron status across the phenome: A mendelian randomization study
references.finding: Higher genetic iron status lowered iron-deficiency anemia and hypercholesterolemia but raised skin and soft-tissue infections (cellulitis/abscess OR 1.25).

references.authors: Timmers PRHJ, Wilson JF, Joshi PK, et al.
references.title: Multivariate genomic scan implicates novel loci and haem metabolism in human ageing
references.n: Multivariate GWAS of healthspan, parental lifespan and longevity
references.finding: Identified haem metabolism as a pathway linked to human ageing traits.

references.authors: Jiang L, Wang K, Lo K, et al.
references.title: Sex-Specific Association of Circulating Ferritin Level and Risk of Type 2 Diabetes: A Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Prospective Studies
references.finding: Each 100 ug/L higher ferritin was associated with 22% higher type 2 diabetes risk, stronger in women (RR 1.53) than men (RR 1.21).

references.authors: Kunutsor SK, Apekey TA, Walley J, et al.
references.title: Ferritin levels and risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective evidence
references.finding: Top vs bottom fifth of ferritin: type 2 diabetes RR 1.73; heme iron intake RR 1.28.

references.authors: Zhao Z, Li S, Liu G, et al.
references.title: Body iron stores and heme-iron intake in relation to risk of type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Highest vs lowest ferritin: prospective T2D RR 1.66; highest vs lowest heme iron intake RR 1.31.

references.authors: Hunnicutt J, He K, Xun P
references.title: Dietary iron intake and body iron stores are associated with risk of coronary heart disease in a meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies
references.finding: Heme iron intake was associated with higher CHD incidence (RR 1.57) while total iron, serum iron and transferrin saturation were inversely associated.

references.authors: Danesh J, Appleby P
references.title: Coronary heart disease and iron status: meta-analyses of prospective studies
references.finding: Ferritin >=200 vs <200 ug/L showed no association with coronary heart disease (RR 1.0, 0.8-1.3); no strong link for any iron marker.

references.authors: Sempos CT, Looker AC, Gillum RE, et al.
references.title: Serum ferritin and death from all causes and cardiovascular disease: the NHANES II Mortality Study. National Health and Nutrition Examination Study
references.finding: Serum ferritin was not associated with cardiovascular or all-cause death in US adults; low ferritin predicted higher mortality in Black men.

references.authors: Wood RJ
references.title: The iron-heart disease connection: is it dead or just hiding?
references.finding: Reviewed why the iron-heart hypothesis remained unresolved and called for better measures of the potentially damaging forms of iron.

references.authors: Fang X, An P, Wang H, et al.
references.title: Dietary intake of heme iron and risk of cardiovascular disease: a dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies
references.finding: Each 1 mg/day of heme iron was associated with 7% higher cardiovascular risk; non-heme and total iron were not associated.

references.authors: Bastide NM, Pierre FH, Corpet DE
references.title: Heme iron from meat and risk of colorectal cancer: a meta-analysis and a review of the mechanisms involved
references.finding: Highest vs lowest heme iron intake: colon cancer RR 1.18; heme catalyses N-nitroso compound formation and lipid peroxidation in the gut.

references.authors: Dixon SJ, Lemberg KM, Lamprecht MR, et al.
references.title: Ferroptosis: an iron-dependent form of nonapoptotic cell death
references.finding: Defined ferroptosis: an iron-dependent, lipid-peroxidation-driven cell death triggered by cystine/glutathione depletion and blocked by ferrostatin-1.

references.authors: Stockwell BR, Friedmann Angeli JP, Bayir H, et al.
references.title: Ferroptosis: A Regulated Cell Death Nexus Linking Metabolism, Redox Biology, and Disease
references.finding: Ferroptosis review: iron, polyunsaturated lipid peroxidation and loss of GPX4/glutathione defences link metabolism, redox biology and disease.

references.authors: Kakhlon O, Cabantchik ZI
references.title: The labile iron pool: characterization, measurement, and participation in cellular processes(1)
references.finding: The labile (chelatable, redox-active) iron pool promotes ROS formation and rises and falls with iron import, chelation and ferritin turnover.

references.authors: Kell DB, Pretorius E
references.title: Serum ferritin is an important inflammatory disease marker, as it is mainly a leakage product from damaged cells
references.finding: Argues serum ferritin is largely a leakage product of damaged cells, explaining its correlation with inflammation and oxidative stress as well as with iron stores.

references.authors: Ullum H, Rostgaard K, Kamper-Jørgensen M, et al.
references.title: Blood donation and blood donor mortality after adjustment for a healthy donor effect
references.finding: Each extra annual donation was linked to 18.6% lower mortality, shrinking to 7.5% after adjusting for the healthy donor effect; not proof of benefit.

references.authors: Atsma F, Veldhuizen I, Verbeek A, et al.
references.title: Healthy donor effect: its magnitude in health research among blood donors
references.finding: Donors were healthier than the general population (better self-rated health, fewer GP visits), demonstrating a strong healthy donor effect.

references.authors: Salonen JT, Tuomainen TP, Salonen R, et al.
references.title: Donation of blood is associated with reduced risk of myocardial infarction. The Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study
references.finding: Men who had donated blood in the previous 24 months had 88% lower risk of acute MI (1 event in 153 donors).

references.authors: Ascherio A, Rimm EB, Giovannucci E, et al.
references.title: Blood donations and risk of coronary heart disease in men
references.finding: Lifetime blood donation lowered ferritin but was not associated with MI or fatal CHD (RR 1.2 for >=30 donations vs never).

references.authors: Houschyar KS, Lüdtke R, Dobos GJ, et al.
references.title: Effects of phlebotomy-induced reduction of body iron stores on metabolic syndrome: results from a randomized clinical trial
references.finding: Removing 550-800 mL blood lowered systolic BP by 16.6 mmHg vs control at 6 weeks, without changing insulin resistance (HOMA).

references.authors: Manco M, Fernandez-Real JM
references.title: Back to past leeches: repeated phlebotomies and cardiovascular risk
references.finding: Commentary on the phlebotomy trial noting design drawbacks (unblinded, short) while discussing iron depletion and metabolic risk.

references.authors: Di Angelantonio E, Thompson SG, Kaptoge S, et al.
references.title: Efficiency and safety of varying the frequency of whole blood donation (INTERVAL): a randomised trial of 45 000 donors
references.finding: INTERVAL: shorter donation intervals collected more blood but caused more symptoms (tiredness, restless legs), lower hemoglobin and ferritin, and more deferrals.

references.authors: Kaptoge S, Di Angelantonio E, Moore C, et al.
references.title: Longer-term efficiency and safety of increasing the frequency of whole blood donation (INTERVAL): extension study of a randomised trial of 20 757 blood donors
references.finding: Each week shorter inter-donation interval lowered ferritin by ~5-6.5% and increased low-hemoglobin deferrals.

references.authors: van den Hurk K, van Kraaij MGJ, Zalpuri S
references.title: Lessons from the INTERVAL study
references.finding: Letter on INTERVAL urging attention to iron deficiency in frequent donors and ferritin monitoring.

references.authors: Hurrell R, Egli I
references.title: Iron bioavailability and dietary reference values
references.finding: Iron bioavailability is ~14-18% from mixed diets and 5-12% from vegetarian diets; body iron status influences absorption more than diet composition.

references.authors: Pasricha SR, Tye-Din J, Muckenthaler MU, et al.
references.title: Iron deficiency
references.finding: Iron deficiency is a leading cause of global disease burden; harms occur even without anaemia; hepcidin limits absorption of high-dose oral iron.

references.authors: Vaucher P, Druais PL, Waldvogel S, et al.
references.title: Effect of iron supplementation on fatigue in nonanemic menstruating women with low ferritin: a randomized controlled trial
references.n: 198 non-anaemic menstruating women with ferritin <50 ug/L
references.finding: 80 mg/day oral iron for 12 weeks reduced fatigue scores by 47.7% vs 28.8% with placebo.

references.authors: Falkingham M, Abdelhamid A, Curtis P, et al.
references.title: The effects of oral iron supplementation on cognition in older children and adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Iron supplements improved attention/concentration and, in anaemic people only, IQ by 2.5 points; trials were small and weak.

references.authors: Fiani D, Chahine S, Zaboube M, et al.
references.title: Psychiatric and cognitive outcomes of iron supplementation in non-anemic children, adolescents, and menstruating adults: A meta-analysis and systematic review
references.finding: In non-anaemic iron-deficient youth and menstruating adults, iron improved anxiety, fatigue and memory; effects vanished when iron-replete people were analysed alone.

references.authors: Finkelstein JL, Cuthbert A, Weeks J, et al.
references.title: Daily oral iron supplementation during pregnancy
references.finding: Daily iron in pregnancy reduces maternal anaemia, iron deficiency and iron-deficiency anaemia at term and probably reduces low birthweight (RR 0.84).

references.authors: Peña-Rosas JP, De-Regil LM, Garcia-Casal MN, et al.
references.title: Daily oral iron supplementation during pregnancy
references.finding: Prenatal iron cut anaemia at term by 70% but raised the risk of haemoglobin above 130 g/L.

references.authors: Hansen R, Sejer EPF, Holm C, et al.
references.title: Iron supplements in pregnant women with normal iron status: A systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Daily iron in iron-replete pregnant women probably reduced iron-deficiency anaemia at term and low birthweight.

references.authors: Rahman MM, Abe SK, Rahman MS, et al.
references.title: Maternal anemia and risk of adverse birth and health outcomes in low- and middle-income countries: systematic review and meta-analysis
references.n: 26 studies in low- and middle-income countries
references.finding: Maternal anaemia was associated with low birthweight (RR 1.31), preterm birth (RR 1.63) and perinatal mortality (RR 1.51).

references.authors: Young MF, Oaks BM, Rogers HP, et al.
references.title: Maternal low and high hemoglobin concentrations and associations with adverse maternal and infant health outcomes: an updated global systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Both low and high maternal haemoglobin were associated with adverse outcomes; high Hb with gestational diabetes (OR 1.71), pre-eclampsia and stillbirth.

references.authors: Khambalia AZ, Aimone A, Nagubandi P, et al.
references.title: High maternal iron status, dietary iron intake and iron supplement use in pregnancy and risk of gestational diabetes mellitus: a prospective study and systematic review
references.finding: Higher ferritin (OR 1.41 per unit), serum iron and heme iron intake were associated with gestational diabetes; two supplement trials showed no association.

references.authors: Sazawal S, Black RE, Ramsan M, et al.
references.title: Effects of routine prophylactic supplementation with iron and folic acid on admission to hospital and mortality in preschool children in a high malaria transmission setting: community-based, randomised, placebo-controlled trial
references.finding: Routine iron (12.5 mg) plus folic acid in a high-malaria setting raised death or hospitalisation by 12%; the arm was stopped early.

references.authors: English M, Snow RW
references.title: Iron and folic acid supplementation and malaria risk
references.finding: Lancet comment on the Pemba trial discussing risks of untargeted iron supplementation where malaria is common.

references.authors: Jaeggi T, Kortman GA, Moretti D, et al.
references.title: Iron fortification adversely affects the gut microbiome, increases pathogen abundance and induces intestinal inflammation in Kenyan infants
references.finding: Iron-containing micronutrient powders increased enterobacteria and pathogenic E. coli, lowered bifidobacteria and raised faecal calprotectin (gut inflammation).

references.authors: Weiss G
references.title: Dietary iron supplementation: a proinflammatory attack on the intestine?
references.finding: Gut commentary describing dietary iron supplementation as a potential pro-inflammatory insult to the intestine.

references.authors: Simonyté Sjödin K, Domellöf M, Lagerqvist C, et al.
references.title: Administration of ferrous sulfate drops has significant effects on the gut microbiota of iron-sufficient infants: a randomised controlled study
references.finding: Ferrous sulfate drops significantly changed the gut microbiota of infants who were not iron deficient.

references.authors: Lund EK, Wharf SG, Fairweather-Tait SJ, et al.
references.title: Oral ferrous sulfate supplements increase the free radical-generating capacity of feces from healthy volunteers
references.finding: 19 mg/day ferrous sulfate for 2 weeks raised weakly bound faecal iron 5-fold and faecal free-radical production by ~40%.

references.authors: Shearer J, Shah S, MacInnis MJ, et al.
references.title: Dose-Responsive Effects of Iron Supplementation on the Gut Microbiota in Middle-Aged Women
references.finding: High-dose iron supplements (>100 mg/day) were associated with more Proteobacteria and fewer butyrate producers (e.g. Faecalibacterium).

references.authors: Pilling LC, Tamosauskaite J, Jones G, et al.
references.title: Common conditions associated with hereditary haemochromatosis genetic variants: cohort study in UK Biobank
references.finding: HFE C282Y homozygosity (1 in 156) was associated with liver disease, arthritis and diabetes; diagnosed haemochromatosis in 21.7% of homozygous men and 9.8% of women.

references.authors: EFSA NDA Panel: Turck D, Bohn T, Castenmiller J, et al.
references.title: Scientific opinion on the tolerable upper intake level for iron
references.finding: EFSA could not set an iron UL; it set a safe level of 40 mg/day total iron for adults including pregnant women.

references.authors: Chavarro JE, Rich-Edwards JW, Rosner BA, et al.
references.title: Iron intake and risk of ovulatory infertility
references.finding: Women using iron supplements had 40% lower risk of ovulatory infertility (RR 0.60); heme iron was unrelated.

references.authors: Hahn KA, Wesselink AK, Wise LA, et al.
references.title: Iron Consumption Is Not Consistently Associated with Fecundability among North American and Danish Pregnancy Planners
references.n: 4662 pregnancy planners (Denmark n=1693, North America n=2969)
references.finding: Iron intake was not consistently associated with fecundability; supplements helped modestly in North America (FR 1.19) and in women with heavy menses.

references.authors: Ammar O, Houas Z, Mehdi M
references.title: The association between iron, calcium, and oxidative stress in seminal plasma and sperm quality
references.finding: Seminal iron was higher in subfertile men and correlated negatively with sperm motility and normal morphology.

references.authors: Perera D, Pizzey A, Campbell A, et al.
references.title: Sperm DNA damage in potentially fertile homozygous beta-thalassaemia patients with iron overload
references.finding: Iron-overloaded men (median ferritin 2251 ug/L) had more sperm DNA damage, which rose with later onset of chelation.

references.authors: Carlomagno F, Tenuta M, Sansone A, et al.
references.title: Iron overload disorders in adults: a comprehensive review of gonadal function, reproductive, and sexual health
references.n: Systematic review: 1201 men, 2134 women with iron overload
references.finding: In iron overload disorders, 47% of men had hypogonadism and over half of those assessed had azoospermia or other sperm abnormalities; early chelation helps prevent but rarely reverses damage.

references.authors: Ni Z, Li Y, Song D, et al.
references.title: Iron-overloaded follicular fluid increases the risk of endometriosis-related infertility by triggering granulosa cell ferroptosis and oocyte dysmaturity
references.finding: Iron-overloaded follicular fluid from women with endometriosis triggered granulosa-cell ferroptosis and impaired oocyte maturation in mouse models; vitamin E and deferoxamine helped.

references.authors: Rayman MP
references.title: Selenium and human health
references.finding: Selenium's health effects follow a U-shaped curve: extra intake may help people with low status but those with adequate-to-high status may be harmed.

references.authors: Rayman MP, Winther KH, Pastor-Barriuso R, et al.
references.title: Effect of long-term selenium supplementation on mortality: Results from a multiple-dose, randomised controlled trial
references.finding: 300 ug/day selenium for 5 years raised all-cause mortality over 10 years (HR 1.59, 1.02-2.46); 100 and 200 ug showed no harm.

references.authors: Hurst R, Armah CN, Dainty JR, et al.
references.title: Establishing optimal selenium status: results of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
references.finding: Selenoprotein P was optimised with ~50 ug/day selenium on top of a ~55 ug/day habitual intake; platelet GPx did not change.

references.authors: Ashton K, Hooper L, Harvey LJ, et al.
references.title: Methods of assessment of selenium status in humans: a systematic review
references.finding: Plasma/whole-blood selenium, selenoprotein P and GPx activity respond to selenium intake and are usable status markers.

references.authors: Zhou H, Wang T, Li Q, et al.
references.title: Prevention of Keshan Disease by Selenium Supplementation: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
references.finding: Selenium supplementation in endemic areas cut Keshan disease (selenium-deficiency cardiomyopathy) incidence by 86% (RR 0.14).

references.authors: Stranges S, Marshall JR, Natarajan R, et al.
references.title: Effects of long-term selenium supplementation on the incidence of type 2 diabetes: a randomized trial
references.finding: 200 ug/day selenium raised type 2 diabetes (HR 1.55), highest in the top baseline selenium tertile (HR 2.70).

references.authors: Bleys J, Navas-Acien A, Guallar E
references.title: Selenium and diabetes: more bad news for supplements
references.finding: Editorial on the NPC diabetes result titled 'more bad news for supplements'.

references.authors: Kristal AR, Darke AK, Morris JS, et al.
references.title: Baseline selenium status and effects of selenium and vitamin e supplementation on prostate cancer risk
references.finding: Selenium raised high-grade prostate cancer by 91% in men with high baseline selenium; vitamin E raised prostate cancer in men with low selenium.

references.authors: Frankel PH, Parker RS, Madsen FC, et al.
references.title: Baseline selenium and prostate cancer risk: comments and open questions
references.finding: Editorial raising open questions about the SELECT baseline-selenium analysis.

references.authors: Vinceti M, Filippini T, Del Giovane C, et al.
references.title: Selenium for preventing cancer
references.finding: Cochrane: selenium supplements did not prevent cancer (RR 1.01, high certainty).

references.authors: EFSA NDA Panel: Turck D, Bohn T, Castenmiller J, et al.
references.title: Scientific opinion on the tolerable upper intake level for selenium
references.finding: EFSA set a selenium UL of 255 ug/day for adults (including pregnancy), based on alopecia in SELECT at 330 ug/day.

references.authors: Fosmire GJ
references.title: Zinc toxicity
references.finding: Zinc at 100-300 mg/day induces copper deficiency with anaemia and neutropenia; even lower doses may impair copper and iron use and lower HDL.

references.authors: Jaiser SR, Winston GP
references.title: Copper deficiency myelopathy
references.finding: Copper deficiency myelopathy mimics B12 deficiency; risk factors include zinc overload, upper GI surgery and malabsorption; cytopenias in 78%.

references.authors: Fischer PW, Giroux A, L'Abbé MR
references.title: Effect of zinc supplementation on copper status in adult man
references.finding: 50 mg/day zinc for 6 weeks lowered erythrocyte Cu,Zn-superoxide dismutase activity, an early sign of reduced copper status.

references.authors: Hosseini R, Ferns GA, Sahebkar A, et al.
references.title: Zinc supplementation is associated with a reduction in serum markers of inflammation and oxidative stress in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: Zinc supplements lowered CRP (-0.92 mg/L), TNF-alpha and malondialdehyde, with very high heterogeneity.

references.authors: Jafari A, Ghobadi S
references.title: Comments on "Zinc supplementation is associated with a reduction in serum markers of inflammation and oxidative stress in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials"
references.finding: Letter criticising the zinc meta-analysis for inadequate search, methodological flaws and interpretation that might bias results.

references.authors: Hosseini R, Ferns GA, Sahebkar A, et al.
references.title: Response to commentary on 'zinc supplementation is associated with a reduction in serum markers of inflammation and oxidative stress in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials'
references.finding: Authors' reply defending their zinc meta-analysis.

references.authors: Wessells KR, Brown KH
references.title: Estimating the global prevalence of zinc deficiency: results based on zinc availability in national food supplies and the prevalence of stunting
references.finding: An estimated 17.3% of the world's population is at risk of inadequate zinc intake, highest in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.

references.authors: Davis CD, Greger JL
references.title: Longitudinal changes of manganese-dependent superoxide dismutase and other indexes of manganese and iron status in women
references.finding: 15 mg/day manganese raised lymphocyte MnSOD activity, showing SOD2 activity responds to manganese supply.

references.authors: Wang Y, Li J, Zhuang J, et al.
references.title: Manganese in health and disease
references.finding: Manganese is the MnSOD cofactor in mitochondria; dysregulated manganese accumulates in brain with neurotoxic effects.

references.authors: McNulty H, Pentieva K, Ward M
references.title: Causes and Clinical Sequelae of Riboflavin Deficiency
references.finding: Subclinical riboflavin deficiency may be widespread even in high-income countries but goes undetected; linked to anaemia and hypertension.

references.authors: Wilson CP, McNulty H, Ward M, et al.
references.title: Blood pressure in treated hypertensive individuals with the MTHFR 677TT genotype is responsive to intervention with riboflavin: findings of a targeted randomized trial
references.finding: 1.6 mg/day riboflavin for 16 weeks lowered systolic BP by 5.6 mmHg vs placebo in this genotype.

references.authors: Veronese N, Pizzol D, Smith L, et al.
references.title: Effect of Magnesium Supplementation on Inflammatory Parameters: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
references.finding: Magnesium supplements lowered serum CRP and raised nitric oxide.

references.authors: Nielsen FH, Johnson LK, Zeng H
references.title: Magnesium supplementation improves indicators of low magnesium status and inflammatory stress in adults older than 51 years with poor quality sleep
references.finding: 320 mg/day magnesium lowered CRP only in those with baseline CRP >3 mg/L; 58% ate below the magnesium EAR.

references.authors: Srinutta T, Chewcharat A, Takkavatakarn K, et al.
references.title: Proton pump inhibitors and hypomagnesemia: A meta-analysis of observational studies
references.finding: PPI use was associated with hypomagnesaemia (adjusted OR 1.71), more with high doses (OR 2.13).

references.authors: DiNicolantonio JJ, O'Keefe JH, Wilson W
references.title: Subclinical magnesium deficiency: a principal driver of cardiovascular disease and a public health crisis
references.finding: Opinion review claiming subclinical magnesium deficiency is a principal driver of cardiovascular disease and a public health crisis (lead author discloses a related book).

references.authors: Levine M, Conry-Cantilena C, Wang Y, et al.
references.title: Vitamin C pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers: evidence for a recommended dietary allowance
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Plasma vitamin C rises steeply between 30 and 100 mg/day, plateaus from 200 mg/day; white cells saturate at 100 mg; doses >400 mg have no evident value; oxalate rises at 1000 mg.

references.authors: Levine M, Wang Y, Padayatty SJ, et al.
references.title: A new recommended dietary allowance of vitamin C for healthy young women
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Plasma and cells saturated at 400 mg/day; F2-isoprostanes did not change at any vitamin C dose in these replete women.

references.authors: Carr AC, Frei B
references.title: Toward a new recommended dietary allowance for vitamin C based on antioxidant and health effects in humans
references.finding: Argued that 90-100 mg/day vitamin C is needed for optimal chronic disease risk reduction and proposed an RDA of 120 mg/day.

references.authors: Schleicher RL, Carroll MD, Ford ES, et al.
references.title: Serum vitamin C and the prevalence of vitamin C deficiency in the United States: 2003-2004 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES)
references.finding: 7.1% of the US population was vitamin C deficient; smokers had about one-third lower concentrations.

references.authors: Traber MG
references.title: Vitamin E inadequacy in humans: causes and consequences
references.finding: >90% of Americans eat less alpha-tocopherol than the EAR; plasma alpha-tocopherol <12 umol/L is linked to infection, anaemia and poor pregnancy outcomes.

references.authors: Miller ER 3rd, Pastor-Barriuso R, Dalal D, et al.
references.title: Meta-analysis: high-dosage vitamin E supplementation may increase all-cause mortality
references.finding: High-dose vitamin E (>=400 IU/day) raised all-cause mortality by 39 per 10,000; risk increased above ~150 IU/day.

references.authors: EFSA NDA Panel: Turck D, Bohn T, Castenmiller J, et al.
references.title: Scientific opinion on the tolerable upper intake level for vitamin E
references.finding: EFSA retained a vitamin E UL of 300 mg/day alpha-tocopherol for adults, based on bleeding risk.

references.authors: Lam JR, Schneider JL, Zhao W, et al.
references.title: Proton pump inhibitor and histamine 2 receptor antagonist use and vitamin B12 deficiency
references.finding: Two or more years of PPIs (OR 1.65) or H2 blockers (OR 1.25) was associated with vitamin B12 deficiency, more at higher PPI doses.

references.authors: Chapman LE, Darling AL, Brown JE
references.title: Association between metformin and vitamin B(12) deficiency in patients with type 2 diabetes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Metformin lowered B12 by about 57 pmol/L, causing deficiency or borderline status in some patients.

references.authors: Niklewicz A, Hannibal L, Warren M, et al.
references.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of functional vitamin B12 status among adult vegans
references.finding: Vegans had lower serum B12 and higher homocysteine and methylmalonic acid than omnivores, indicating functional B12 deficiency.

references.authors: Martí-Carvajal AJ, Solà I, Lathyris D, et al.
references.title: Homocysteine-lowering interventions for preventing cardiovascular events
references.finding: Cochrane: B-vitamin homocysteine lowering did not reduce MI or death but modestly reduced stroke (RR 0.90).

references.authors: Huo Y, Li J, Qin X, et al.
references.title: Efficacy of folic acid therapy in primary prevention of stroke among adults with hypertension in China: the CSPPT randomized clinical trial
references.finding: CSPPT: enalapril plus 0.8 mg folic acid cut first stroke by 21% (HR 0.79) vs enalapril alone in a population without folate fortification.

references.authors: Stampfer M, Willett W
references.title: Folate supplements for stroke prevention: targeted trial trumps the rest
references.finding: JAMA editorial arguing that the CSPPT targeted trial in a low-folate population outweighs earlier null trials in fortified populations.

references.authors: Ebbing M, Bønaa KH, Nygård O, et al.
references.title: Cancer incidence and mortality after treatment with folic acid and vitamin B12
references.finding: Folic acid (0.8 mg) plus B12 raised cancer incidence (HR 1.21), cancer death (HR 1.38) and all-cause death (HR 1.18) in an unfortified population.

references.authors: Drake BF, Colditz GA
references.title: Assessing cancer prevention studies--a matter of time
references.finding: Editorial on the Norwegian folic acid/B12 cancer finding discussing timing and interpretation of cancer prevention trials.

references.authors: Cole BF, Baron JA, Sandler RS, et al.
references.title: Folic acid for the prevention of colorectal adenomas: a randomized clinical trial
references.finding: 1 mg/day folic acid did not reduce colorectal adenomas and may have raised advanced lesions (RR 1.67, P = .05).

references.authors: EFSA NDA Panel: Turck D, Bohn T, Castenmiller J, et al.
references.title: Scientific opinion on the tolerable upper intake level for folate
references.finding: EFSA retained a 1000 ug/day UL for synthetic folic acid in adults, based on masking/progression of B12-deficiency neuropathy; cancer links judged insufficient.

references.authors: Bath SC, Steer CD, Golding J, et al.
references.title: Effect of inadequate iodine status in UK pregnant women on cognitive outcomes in their children: results from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC)
references.finding: Children of mothers with iodine:creatinine <150 ug/g had higher odds of low verbal IQ (OR 1.58) and poor reading scores.

references.authors: Stagnaro-Green A, Pearce EN
references.title: Iodine and pregnancy: a call to action
references.finding: Lancet comment calling for action on iodine nutrition in pregnancy.

references.authors: Mills JL, Buck Louis GM, Kannan K, et al.
references.title: Delayed conception in women with low-urinary iodine concentrations: a population-based prospective cohort study
references.finding: Women with iodine:creatinine <50 ug/g had 46% lower fecundability per cycle (OR 0.54).

references.authors: Sohn SY, Inoue K, Rhee CM, et al.
references.title: Risks of Iodine Excess
references.finding: Excess iodine (supplements, contrast media, amiodarone) can trigger hypo- or hyperthyroidism in susceptible people.

references.authors: Alexander EK, Pearce EN, Brent GA, et al.
references.title: 2017 Guidelines of the American Thyroid Association for the Diagnosis and Management of Thyroid Disease During Pregnancy and the Postpartum
references.finding: ATA 2017 pregnancy guideline including recommendations on iodine nutrition before and during pregnancy and lactation.

references.authors: Korevaar TIM, Leung AM, Alexander EK, et al.
references.title: American Thyroid Association 2026 Guidelines for Thyroid Disease in Preconception, Pregnancy, and Postpartum
references.finding: ATA 2026 update of the pregnancy, preconception and postpartum thyroid guideline, including iodine supplementation recommendations.

references.authors: Rothman KJ, Moore LL, Singer MR, et al.
references.title: Teratogenicity of high vitamin A intake
references.finding: Supplemental preformed vitamin A >10,000 IU/day was associated with a 4.8-fold prevalence of cranial-neural-crest birth defects.

references.authors: Wu AM, Huang CQ, Lin ZK, et al.
references.title: The relationship between vitamin A and risk of fracture: meta-analysis of prospective studies
references.n: 8 intake studies (283,930 participants) and 4 blood studies
references.finding: High retinol intake was associated with higher hip fracture risk (RR 1.40); beta-carotene was not; both high and low blood retinol were risky.

references.authors: EFSA NDA Panel: Turck D, Bohn T, Castenmiller J, et al.
references.title: Scientific opinion on the tolerable upper intake level for preformed vitamin A and β-carotene
references.finding: EFSA retained a 3000 ug RE/day UL for preformed vitamin A, based on teratogenicity.

references.authors: Institute of Medicine (US) Standing Committee on the Scientific Evaluation of Dietary Reference Intakes
references.title: Dietary Reference Intakes for Calcium, Phosphorus, Magnesium, Vitamin D, and Fluoride
references.finding: IOM DRI report for calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, vitamin D and fluoride (magnesium RDA 310-420 mg; UL 350 mg from supplements).

references.authors: Institute of Medicine (US) Standing Committee on the Scientific Evaluation of Dietary Reference Intakes and its Panel on Folate, Other B Vitamins, and Choline
references.title: Dietary Reference Intakes for Thiamin, Riboflavin, Niacin, Vitamin B(6), Folate, Vitamin B(12), Pantothenic Acid, Biotin, and Choline
references.finding: IOM DRI report for B vitamins and choline (riboflavin, folate, B12; folic acid UL 1000 ug; no UL for riboflavin or B12).

references.authors: Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Dietary Antioxidants and Related Compounds
references.title: Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin C, Vitamin E, Selenium, and Carotenoids
references.finding: IOM DRI report for vitamin C, vitamin E, selenium and carotenoids (ULs: vitamin C 2000 mg, vitamin E 1000 mg, selenium 400 ug).

references.authors: Institute of Medicine (US) Panel on Micronutrients
references.title: Dietary Reference Intakes for Vitamin A, Vitamin K, Arsenic, Boron, Chromium, Copper, Iodine, Iron, Manganese, Molybdenum, Nickel, Silicon, Vanadium, and Zinc
references.finding: IOM DRI report for vitamin A, copper, iodine, iron, manganese, zinc and others (ULs: zinc 40 mg, copper 10 mg, iron 45 mg, iodine 1100 ug, manganese 11 mg, preformed vitamin A 3000 ug).

references.authors: EFSA Scientific Committee on Food / Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies
references.title: Tolerable Upper Intake Levels for Vitamins and Minerals
references.finding: EFSA/SCF compendium of tolerable upper intake levels (e.g. zinc 25 mg, copper 5 mg, iodine 600 ug, supplemental magnesium 250 mg per day for adults).

references.authors: Passarelli S, Free CM, Shepon A, et al.
references.title: Global estimation of dietary micronutrient inadequacies: a modelling analysis
references.finding: From food alone, >5 billion people under-consume iodine, vitamin E and calcium and >4 billion under-consume iron, riboflavin, folate and vitamin C.

references.authors: Sesso HD, Rist PM, Aragaki AK, et al.
references.title: Multivitamins in the prevention of cancer and cardiovascular disease: the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study (COSMOS) randomized clinical trial
references.finding: A daily multivitamin for a median 3.6 years did not reduce total cancer (HR 0.97) or CVD (HR 0.98); lung cancer was lower (HR 0.62).

references.authors: Gaziano JM, Sesso HD, Christen WG, et al.
references.title: Multivitamins in the prevention of cancer in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
references.finding: A daily multivitamin modestly reduced total cancer (HR 0.92) over a median 11.2 years.

references.authors: Sesso HD, Christen WG, Bubes V, et al.
references.title: Multivitamins in the prevention of cardiovascular disease in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
references.finding: A daily multivitamin did not reduce major cardiovascular events (HR 1.01) or total mortality (HR 0.94).

references.authors: Bach PB, Lewis RJ
references.title: Multiplicities in the assessment of multiple vitamins: is it too soon to tell men that vitamins prevent cancer?
references.finding: JAMA editorial questioning whether the PHS II cancer result, given multiple comparisons, justified telling men vitamins prevent cancer.

references.authors: Grodstein F, O'Brien J, Kang JH, et al.
references.title: Long-term multivitamin supplementation and cognitive function in men: a randomized trial
references.finding: Long-term multivitamin use did not slow cognitive decline.

references.authors: Vyas CM, Manson JE, Sesso HD, et al.
references.title: Effect of multivitamin-mineral supplementation versus placebo on cognitive function: results from the clinic subcohort of the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study (COSMOS) randomized clinical trial and meta-analysis of 3 cognitive studies within COSMOS
references.n: 573 COSMOS-Clinic participants plus meta-analysis of 3 COSMOS cohorts
references.finding: A multivitamin improved episodic memory over 2 years; pooled COSMOS data showed small benefits on global cognition (0.07 SD).

references.authors: Loftfield E, O'Connell CP, Abnet CC, et al.
references.title: Multivitamin Use and Mortality Risk in 3 Prospective US Cohorts
references.finding: Daily multivitamin use was not associated with lower mortality (HR 1.04 in the first half of follow-up).

references.authors: Barnard ND, Kahleova H, Becker R
references.title: The Limited Value of Multivitamin Supplements
references.finding: Commentary on the cohort study arguing that multivitamins have limited value for healthy people.

references.authors: Mangione CM, Barry MJ, Nicholson WK, et al.
references.title: Vitamin, Mineral, and Multivitamin Supplementation to Prevent Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
references.finding: USPSTF: insufficient evidence for multivitamins to prevent CVD or cancer; recommends against beta-carotene and vitamin E.

references.authors: O'Connor EA, Evans CV, Ivlev I, et al.
references.title: Vitamin and Mineral Supplements for the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force
references.finding: Multivitamins were associated with slightly lower cancer incidence (OR 0.93, 4 RCTs) with important limitations; beta-carotene raised lung cancer; limited evidence linked vitamin A to hip fracture, vitamin E to hemorrhagic stroke and vitamin C to kidney stones.

references.authors: Schisterman EF, Sjaarda LA, Clemons T, et al.
references.title: Effect of Folic Acid and Zinc Supplementation in Men on Semen Quality and Live Birth Among Couples Undergoing Infertility Treatment: A Randomized Clinical Trial
references.n: 2370 men in couples seeking infertility care (FAZST)
references.finding: 5 mg folic acid plus 30 mg zinc for 6 months did not improve semen quality or live birth (34% vs 35%) and slightly raised sperm DNA fragmentation (+2.4 points).

references.authors: Jenkins T, Aston K, Carrell D, et al.
references.title: The impact of zinc and folic acid supplementation on sperm DNA methylation: results from the folic acid and zinc supplementation randomized clinical trial (FAZST)
references.finding: Folic acid plus zinc did not significantly change sperm DNA methylation patterns.

references.authors: Zhao J, Dong X, Hu X, et al.
references.title: Zinc levels in seminal plasma and their correlation with male infertility: A systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Infertile men had lower seminal zinc; pooled small trials suggested zinc improved volume, motility and morphology.

references.authors: Buhling K, Schumacher A, Eulenburg CZ, et al.
references.title: Influence of oral vitamin and mineral supplementation on male infertility: a meta-analysis and systematic review
references.finding: Selenium (100-200 ug/day), CoQ10 and carnitines improved semen parameters in small trials; pregnancy data were scarce.

references.authors: Smits RM, Mackenzie-Proctor R, Yazdani A, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants for male subfertility
references.finding: Cochrane: antioxidants may raise live birth (OR 1.79) but evidence was low quality and the effect disappeared when high-risk-of-bias studies were removed.

references.authors: de Ligny W, Smits RM, Mackenzie-Proctor R, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants for male subfertility
references.finding: Cochrane update: possible live birth increase (OR 1.43, very low certainty), no effect in low-risk-of-bias trials.

references.authors: Safarinejad MR, Safarinejad S
references.title: Efficacy of selenium and/or N-acetyl-cysteine for improving semen parameters in infertile men: a double-blind, placebo controlled, randomized study
references.finding: Reported that 200 ug selenium and/or 600 mg NAC improved all semen parameters; the journal issued an Expression of Concern in 2023.

references.authors: Safarinejad MR, Safarinejad S
references.title: Expression of Concern: Efficacy of Selenium and/or N-Acetyl-Cysteine for Improving Semen Parameters in Infertile Men: A Double-Blind, Placebo Controlled, Randomized Study
references.finding: Journal of Urology Expression of Concern regarding the Safarinejad selenium/NAC trial.

references.authors: Scott R, MacPherson A, Yates RW, et al.
references.title: The effect of oral selenium supplementation on human sperm motility
references.n: 69 subfertile Scottish men with low selenium status
references.finding: Selenium (100 ug/day) for 3 months raised sperm motility vs placebo; 11% achieved paternity vs none on placebo.

references.authors: Ursini F, Heim S, Kiess M, et al.
references.title: Dual function of the selenoprotein PHGPx during sperm maturation
references.finding: The selenoprotein PHGPx (GPX4) becomes a structural protein making up >=50% of the sperm midpiece mitochondrial capsule, explaining midpiece fragility in selenium deficiency.

references.authors: Gaskins AJ, Chiu YH, Williams PL, et al.
references.title: Association between serum folate and vitamin B-12 and outcomes of assisted reproductive technologies
references.finding: Highest vs lowest quartile of serum B12 (>701 pg/mL) doubled live birth probability (RR 2.04); folate and B12 above the median together raised live birth by 26 points.

references.authors: Chavarro JE, Rich-Edwards JW, Rosner BA, et al.
references.title: Use of multivitamins, intake of B vitamins, and risk of ovulatory infertility
references.finding: Multivitamin use 6+ times a week was associated with 41% lower ovulatory infertility (RR 0.59), partly explained by folic acid.

references.authors: Cueto HT, Riis AH, Hatch EE, et al.
references.title: Folic acid supplementation and fecundability: a Danish prospective cohort study
references.finding: Folic acid supplement users had 15% higher fecundability (FR 1.15).

references.authors: Penzias A, Azziz R, Bendikson K, et al.
references.title: Optimizing natural fertility: a committee opinion
references.finding: ASRM committee opinion on optimizing natural fertility, including preconception folic acid.

references.authors: Barry MJ, Nicholson WK, Silverstein M, et al.
references.title: Folic Acid Supplementation to Prevent Neural Tube Defects: US Preventive Services Task Force Reaffirmation Recommendation Statement
references.finding: USPSTF (A recommendation): everyone who could become pregnant should take 400-800 ug folic acid daily.
